tips.title: Use the ANS key
tips.body: Type the formula once with **ANS** where the $x$ goes, then press equals repeatedly. It is faster than retyping and it removes the rounding error that costs most of the marks.

tips.title: x₀ is the value you are given
tips.body: $x_0$ is the starting value from the question; $x_1$ is the first value the formula produces. A question asking for $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ wants all three written down.

tips.title: Two iterates agreeing, then stop
tips.body: Keep going until two consecutive values agree to the accuracy asked for, and say that they do. If the values **grow** instead of settling, the rearrangement diverges and another is needed.

steps.title: When you cannot solve it exactly
steps.body:
Some equations have no neat solution. $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$ cannot be factorised and has no formula you are given, yet it certainly has a solution: the graph crosses the $x$-axis.

**Iteration** finds that solution to as many decimal places as you like, by guessing and improving. The method is:

1. **Rearrange** the equation into the form $x = \text{something involving } x$.
2. Put a **starting value** $x_0$ into the right-hand side.
3. The answer out is $x_1$. Put **that** back in to get $x_2$, and keep going.

Written as a formula this is $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$, and the subscripts are just labels: $x_0$ is the guess you were given, $x_1$ the first answer out, and so on.

When the values stop changing to the accuracy you want, you have your solution.

steps.title: Running an iteration
steps.body:
Solve $x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0$ using $x_{n+1} = \dfrac{x_n^2 + 3}{5}$, starting at $x_0 = 0.6$.

The golden rule: **never round part way through**. Keep the full value on your calculator and use the **ANS** key, rounding only the answer you write down.

steps.title: Rearranging into an iterative formula
steps.body:
Exam questions usually hand you the formula, but they also ask you to **show** where it came from. That is pure algebra: get one $x$ on its own on the left.

Take $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$.

steps.text: Start from $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$
Move the other terms across: $x^3 = 2x + 5$
steps.note: the cube alone on the left

steps.text: Take the cube root of both sides: $x = \sqrt[3]{2x + 5}$
So the iteration is $x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{2x_n + 5}$

steps.title: Showing a solution lies between two values
steps.body:
Before or after iterating, a question often asks you to **show** that a solution lies between two numbers. That is a different method: the **sign change**.

If $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have **opposite signs**, and the graph is unbroken between them, it must cross zero somewhere in between. So there is a solution between $a$ and $b$.

steps.title: Rounding, and when to stop
steps.body:
Two habits decide whether you get the marks.

**Never round part way through.** Every rounding error feeds into the next iterate and grows. Use the **ANS** key: type the formula once with ANS in place of $x$, then press equals repeatedly.

**Stop when the answer is stable to the accuracy asked for.** If a question wants 3 decimal places, keep going until two consecutive iterates **agree to 3 decimal places**, then give that value. For the first example, $x_4 = 0.6967$ and $x_5 = 0.6971$ both round to 0.697, so 0.697 is the answer.

Write the iterates down as you go. A question asking for $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ wants all three, and they carry the marks even if the last one slips.

steps.title: Your turn: rearrange, iterate, check
steps.body:
Take the equation $x^3 = 2x + 5$.

1. Show that it rearranges to $x = \sqrt[3]{2x + 5}$.
2. Starting at $x_0 = 2$, work out $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ to 4 decimal places.
3. Show that a solution lies between 2 and 2.1 using a sign change.
4. Give the solution to 3 decimal places.

Use ANS on your calculator and do not round until the last line.

steps.title: Going deeper: when the iteration runs away
steps.body:
Not every rearrangement works. The same equation can be rearranged several ways, and some of them **diverge**: the values grow instead of settling.

Take $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$ again, but rearranged the other way: $2x = x^3 - 5$, so $x = \dfrac{x^3 - 5}{2}$. Starting at $x_0 = 2$ that gives 2, 1.5, -0.813, -2.768, and it keeps running away. The solution is still 2.0946, but this formula will never find it.

**Why.** Near the solution, an iteration converges when the right-hand side changes **more slowly** than $x$ does, and diverges when it changes faster. Cubing makes it change much faster, so that version diverges; taking a cube root makes it change more slowly, so that version converges.

You are not asked to prove this. You are asked to **notice** it: if the values are growing or jumping about, the rearrangement is wrong for the job, and the mark comes from saying so and trying another.

props.title: Same equation, same start, opposite behaviour

visuals.alt: A table comparing two rearrangements of the same equation, one converging to two point zero nine four six and one running away

The solution itself has not changed, only the method of finding it

check.prompt: An iteration gives $x_1 = 1.5$, $x_2 = -0.8$, $x_3 = -2.8$, growing at each step. What should you conclude?
check.solution: Values that grow instead of settling mean the **rearrangement diverges**. The equation still has its solution; this formula just will not find it.
options: This rearrangement diverges, so another is needed
The equation has no solution
The starting value was too small
The solution is negative

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Iteration** finds a solution numerically when the equation cannot be solved exactly.
- Rearrange to $x = \text{something in } x$, then run $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$ from the given $x_0$.
- $x_0$ is the **starting value given to you**; $x_1$ is the first value out.
- **Never round part way through.** Use ANS and round only the final answer.
- **Stop** when two consecutive iterates agree to the accuracy asked for.
- A **sign change** in $f(x)$ between $a$ and $b$ shows a solution lies between them. Substitute both, state both signs, and say *sign change*.
- Some rearrangements **diverge**. If the values grow or jump about, say so and use a different rearrangement.
- Worked here: $x = \dfrac{x^2+3}{5}$ from $x_0 = 0.6$ settles at **0.697**, and $x = \sqrt[3]{2x+5}$ from $x_0 = 2$ settles at **2.095** to 3 d.p..

questions.prompt: An iteration is $x_{n+1} = \dfrac{x_n^2 + 3}{5}$ with $x_0 = 0.6$. Work out $x_2$ to 4 decimal places.
Show that $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$ has a solution between 2 and 2.1, then use $x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{2x_n + 5}$ with $x_0 = 2$ to find that solution to 3 decimal places.
questions.solution: Let f of x be x cubed minus two x minus five. Substituting two gives eight minus four minus five, which is minus one, and substituting two point one gives nine point two six one minus four point two minus five, which is nought point zero six one. One is negative and the other is positive, so there is a sign change, and since the graph is continuous it must cross zero between two and two point one. There is therefore a solution in that interval. Running the iteration from two gives two point zero eight zero one, then two point zero nine two four, then two point zero nine four two, then two point zero nine four five, then two point zero nine four five again. The last two agree to three decimal places, so the solution is two point zero nine five to three decimal places.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The sign change.** Let $f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5$.

$$f(2) = 8 - 4 - 5 = -1 \qquad f(2.1) = 9.261 - 4.2 - 5 = 0.061$$

One is **negative** and the other **positive**, so there is a **sign change**. The graph is continuous, so it must cross zero between them: a solution lies between 2 and 2.1.

**The iteration**, from $x_0 = 2$:

| | |
|---|---|
| $x_1$ | 2.0801 |
| $x_2$ | 2.0924 |
| $x_3$ | 2.0942 |
| $x_4$ | 2.0945 |
| $x_5$ | 2.0945 |

$x_4$ and $x_5$ agree to 3 decimal places, so the solution is $\mathbf{2.095}$.

questions.prompt: A student rearranges $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$ as $x = \dfrac{x^3 - 5}{2}$ and iterates from $x_0 = 2$, getting 1.5, then −0.8, then −2.8. Explain what has happened and what they should do.
questions.solution: The values are not settling towards anything: they are moving further from the starting value at each step and growing in size. That means this rearrangement diverges, so however many steps the student takes it will never reach the solution. The equation itself still has a solution between two and two point one; only the formula is at fault. The student should rearrange the equation a different way, for example as x equals the cube root of two x plus five, which converges, and iterate from the same starting value.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What has happened.** The values are not settling: each one is further from the last and growing in size. This rearrangement **diverges**, so however many steps the student takes it will never reach the solution.

**The equation is fine.** There is still a solution between 2 and 2.1. Only the **formula** is at fault, because cubing makes the right-hand side change much faster than $x$ does.

**What to do.** Rearrange a different way. Writing $x^3 = 2x + 5$ and cube rooting gives $x = \sqrt[3]{2x + 5}$, which **converges** from the same starting value.

examTechnique.body:
Use the ANS key. Type the right-hand side once with ANS where the $x$ goes, press equals, and keep pressing. It is faster than retyping and it removes the rounding error that costs most of the marks in this topic.

Write every iterate down to more decimal places than the question wants. A question asking for $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ is paying for all three.

For a *show that it rearranges* question, write the algebra line by line. The answer is given, so the working is the only thing being marked.

For a *show that a solution lies between* question, substitute **both** values, write both results with their signs, and use the words **sign change**. Do not iterate: that is a different question.

Stop when two consecutive iterates agree to the accuracy asked for, and say that they do.

If the values grow or jump around, do not keep going. Say the rearrangement diverges and, if the question allows, use another.
examinerErrors: Rounding each iterate before feeding it back in, so the error compounds.
Giving only the final value when the question asked for x₁, x₂ and x₃.
Confusing x₀ with x₁: the starting value you are given is x₀.
Iterating when the question asked to show a solution lies between two values, which needs a sign change instead.
Substituting into the rearranged form rather than into f(x) when testing for a sign change.
Not writing the words sign change, or not stating both signs.
Stopping too early, when the iterates agree only to two decimal places but three were asked for.
Carrying on for many steps when the values are clearly diverging.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer uses ANS throughout and never rounds until the final line, writing each iterate to more places than the question needs. For a sign change it substitutes into f(x) rather than the rearranged form, states both values with their signs, uses the phrase sign change and adds that the graph is continuous. It stops when two consecutive iterates agree to the accuracy asked for and says so rather than leaving it implied. Shown a diverging iteration it recognises the behaviour at once, says the rearrangement is at fault rather than the equation, and offers a rearrangement that would converge.
